sentences.text: The animal possessed a long and narrow snout.
Its nasal bones extended forward to the very edge of the fused nostril opening, a trait that serves as the main diagnostic feature of the genus.
Per Ove Persson identified this forward extension of the nasal bone to the fenestra exonarina communis as the primary distinguishing characteristic.
The lower jaw joint was exceptionally long, measuring 13.8 centimetres, and this length was reached by the splenial bone.
The broadened part of the skull was 7.1 centimetres wide at its widest point and 4.7 centimetres wide at the notches.
Unlike modern crocodylians with long, slender teeth, Aigialosuchus had stout and short teeth.
These teeth were somewhat recurved and possessed cylindrical roots.
The surface of the teeth was densely striated with ridges running from base to tip.
A single blunt, wide tooth from Faxe, Denmark, might belong to Aigialosuchus or an alligatoroid genus.
Only one fossil occurrence of Aigialosuchus has been recorded in the scientific literature.
The only species, A. villandensis, was described in 1959 by Per Ove Persson from fossils found in the Kristianstad Basin in southern Sweden.
Swedish paleontologist Per-Ove Persson described the animal in 1959 based on fossils from the Ivö Klack locality in the Kristianstad Basin.
The genus Aigialosuchus was named by Persson in 1960.
Aigialosuchus likely fed on large fish and invertebrates, an adaptation suggested by its short, stout teeth.
Einarsson suggested Aigialosuchus fed on various fish, ammonites, belemnites, and benthic macroinvertebrates based on its robust teeth.
The presence of Aigialosuchus at Ivö Klack suggests it may have preferred coastal waters to lay eggs on adjacent land and bask, similar to modern crocodilians.
Persson originally classified Aigialosuchus as a true crocodile within the subfamily Crocodylinae.
In 2001, Christopher Brochu suggested Aigialosuchus was probably a eusuchian, the group containing all living crocodilians.
Elisabeth Einarsson classified Aigialosuchus as a dyrosaurid in a 2018 paper.
Since 2016, Aigialosuchus has been repeatedly classified within the basal family Dyrosauridae rather than as a eusuchian.
The type species of the genus Aigialosuchus is Aigialosuchus villandensis.
Aigialosuchus lived during the Early Campanian stage.
Aigialosuchus lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
During the Cretaceous, the Ivö Klack site where most Aigialosuchus fossils were found was a small, rocky island in a shallow sea covering southern Scandinavia.
Fossils of Aigialosuchus have only been recovered from Campanian-age deposits in the Kristianstad Basin in Sweden.
It is debated whether the precise classification of Aigialosuchus is certain due to fragmentary remains.
Researchers note that the precise systematic position of Aigialosuchus within Crocodylomorpha remains unclear until a taxonomic revision is performed.
